Arthur Conan Doyle. A Scottish writer and physician best known as the creator of Sherlock Holmes, whose detective stories revolutionized the mystery genre and made Holmes the most famous fictional character of his era. Doyle trained as a doctor and practiced medicine, an experience that informed his character's precision, his understanding of poison and anatomy, and his occasional frustration with public adulation overshadowing his other literary work. He first introduced Sherlock Holmes in the eighteen eighty-seven novel A Study in Scarlet. Holmes then appeared in serialized short stories beginning in eighteen ninety-one, becoming an immediate sensation. The eighteen ninety-two collection The Adventures of Sherlock Holmes cemented Holmes's place in popular culture. The stories popularized detective fiction and established conventions—the brilliant deducer, the loyal companion-narrator, the seemingly impossible case solved through logic—that defined the genre. Despite Holmes's enormous success, Doyle attempted to kill off the character in The Final Problem, published in eighteen ninety-three, having the detective apparently fall to his death at Reichenbach Falls while battling the criminal mastermind Professor Moriarty. This story revealed Moriarty as Holmes's nemesis and arch-rival. Public outcry was so fierce that Doyle eventually resurrected Holmes, returning him in nineteen hundred and one with The Hound of the Baskervilles, one of his most celebrated tales, blending Gothic atmosphere with Holmesian deduction. Beyond Holmes, Doyle wrote historical novels, tales of adventure including The Lost World, featuring a dinosaur-filled plateau, and science fiction, but none achieved Holmes's cultural penetration. Later in life, Doyle was fascinated by spiritualism, writing works defending the spiritualist movement and investigating alleged mediums; this preoccupation sometimes overshadowed his fiction writing. Yet his greatest legacy remains his creation of Sherlock Holmes, a character so vivid and compelling that Doyle himself became secondary to his creation's fame.
